title: Good Masters! Sweet Ladies! Voices from a Medieval Village
author: Laura Amy Schlitz
source: Good Masters! Sweet Ladies! Voices from a Medieval Village (Candlewick Press, 2007)
citation: Schlitz, Laura Amy. Good Masters! Sweet Ladies! Voices from a Medieval Village. Illustrated by Robert Byrd, Candlewick Press, 2007.

sections.heading: Hugo, the Lord's Nephew & Taggot, the Blacksmith's Daughter

epigraph.quote: Good masters, sweet ladies, hear my tale. We lived beneath the shadow of the manor wall, bound to the soil and the season's turn.

paragraphs: In 1255, in an English manor village, twenty-two young voices bring feudal society to vibrant life through dramatic monologues and dialogues in verse and prose. From noble lords' sons in cold stone towers to dirty peasants sleeping in thatched wattle-and-daub huts, the collection explores how young people grappled with social class, physical hardship, and personal dreams.

In 'Hugo, the Lord's Nephew,' a highborn boy recounts his terrifying encounter hunting a wild boar in the lord's forest: his spear slips, his breath catches, and for a fleeting second, he realizes that aristocratic lineage offers no protection against the raw savagery of nature. Directly contrasting Hugo's privilege is 'Taggot, the Blacksmith's Daughter.' Big-boned, shy, and soot-streaked, Taggot hides behind the bellows of her father's forge, yearning for tenderness. When Hugo rides by and hands her a stray spray of hawthorn blossoms, a small spark of human beauty pierces her harsh working-class existence.

sections.heading: Will, the Plowboy & Alice, the Shepherd's Daughter

epigraph.quote: The earth is hard in winter, and the plow is heavy. But the song of the lark rises above the furrows.

paragraphs: In 'Will, the Plowboy,' Will describes the grinding poverty of serfdom—walking barefoot behind the heavy iron plow in freezing spring mud, driven by his harsh stepfather's blows. He works without wages, knowing that half of everything his family harvests belongs to the lord of the manor. Yet even in servitude, Will finds pride in cutting straight furrows across the land.

In 'Alice, the Shepherd's Daughter,' Alice sings a tender lullaby to an orphaned lamb she carries in her rough apron through a freezing storm. Through these distinct voices, Schlitz demonstrates that while thirteenth-century medieval youth faced rigid class adversity, disease, and feudal bondage, their longings—for respect, artistic expression, autonomy, and love—are fundamentally identical to our own.
